items.title: Stands on their tiptoes without help.
Stands on one leg with some help.
Climbs with ease, such as on a playground ladder or steps.
Bends forward without falling.
Sits on a small chair on their own.
Balances on one foot for two seconds or more.
Tiptoes for five steps.
Rides a tricycle.
Uses words with the letter M, like 'mommy' or 'moon'.
Uses words with the letter P, like 'pass' or 'drop'.
Says simple words with the letter T, like 'toy' or 'mat'.
Says simple words with the letter N, like 'nap' or 'banana'.
Says simple words with the letter B, like 'bye' or 'baby'.
Says simple words with the letter Y, like 'yes' or 'year'.
Says simple words with the letter D, like 'mad' or 'day'.
Says simple words with the letter K, like 'keys' or 'okay'.
Says simple words with the letter G, like 'dog' or 'get'.
Says simple words with the letter F (like 'fish' or 'if').
Plays make-believe, like feeding a doll.
Brings other people or pets into imaginative games.
Engages in pretend play, like dressing up or acting like a firefighter.
Has toys 'talk' during pretend play.
Assigns roles in make-believe play with others.
Acts out stories following a clear order.
Makes up things or people in pretend play.
Mixes real and fantasy topics when talking.
Picks up speed when moving around, similar to running.
Runs with direction.
Runs with confidence on different surfaces, like concrete and grass.
Knows how to stop when running.
Arms move in the opposite direction of legs while running.
Runs with bent elbows.
Can make quick turns while running, without falling or stopping.
Stops a rolling ball with hands or body.
Retrieves items after throwing them.
Tries to catch a ball by extending their arms forward.
Bounces a ball on the floor.
Throws a ball overhand within 10 feet (3 meters).
Catches a big ball with their arms and stays steady.
Throws a big ball over their head with both hands.
When throwing, uses the body to aim (shifts weight, moves arm).
Catches a bounced ball.
Catches a ball with just their hands in the air.
Refers to caregivers as 'mama' or 'papa.'
Tries to copy the words you say.
Imitates a sound like 'pa' after you say it.
Copies animal sounds.
Says at least one word with meaning, like saying 'hi' or 'coo' for 'cookie.'
Names one or two foods.
Tries to say the letter T by putting their tongue behind their teeth.
Names familiar objects when asked.
Repeats words overheard in conversation.
Says four or more words.
Repeats names of body parts when they're said.
Names more than three body parts.
Uses possessive words, such as 'mine'.
Names everyday things correctly.
Is able to pronounce ten or more words.
Names smaller body parts (e.g., elbow and eyebrows).
Speaks around 50 words.
Looks at things or people when called by name.
Knows what 'no' means.
Understands three-word phrases, like 'Look, a dog!'
Gives you something when you ask for it.
Answers simple questions with signs, actions, or words.
Points to things they know when you say their name.
Points to caregivers, like 'Mom' or 'Dad'.
Names at least three objects correctly.
Can point to at least one body part when asked.
Matches animal sounds with the right pictures, like pointing to a dog when you say 'woof'.
Knows roughly 100 to 300 everyday words.
Understands everyday actions, like play, run.
Names things by their sounds, like saying 'phone' when it rings.
Describes characteristics of objects, animals, or people (e.g., says 'red' and points at a red ball).
Responds to basic 'who?,' 'what?,' and 'where?' questions.
Uses fingers to tell their age.
Answers simple questions about a story.
Copies easy actions, like shaking a rattle.
Copies facial expressions.
Imitates simple gestures after seeing them.
Imitates what friends do in play, such as building towers when they do.
Moves a body part when asked to.
Copies how adults use things (like pretending to talk on the phone after seeing mom do it).
Copies what caregivers do, like taking a toy phone from a purse and saying 'hello.'
Mimics hand gestures, such as clapping, waving, and pointing.
Swings arms in circles or side to side, copying your moves.
Copies everyday sounds, like a car or phone.
Imitates family members during play.
Copies what adults do when playing, like pretends to rock and feed a doll like a baby.
Enjoys playing on their own.
Gets upset when playtime is interrupted.
Explores on their own with a caregiver nearby.
Can correctly use some everyday items (like sipping from a cup or dialing a phone).
Can feed independently, with or without utensils.
Can use a spoon independently.
Helps with everyday chores, such as cleaning up toys.
Pulls things closer to them.
Lets go of things they're holding on purpose.
Uses both hands together to manipulate objects, like opening a box.
Wrinkles paper using both hands.
Rips paper with both hands.
Starts and stops a toy on their own.
Opens and closes doors and drawers using the handles.
Moves toys with wheels.
Knocks down block towers.
Uses one thing to move or push something else.
Holds two objects with one hand.
Stacks two or more blocks to make a tower.
Screws and unscrews a bottle cap.
Turns things that spin, like toy knobs or faucets.
Stacks three or more blocks.
Presses clay between their hands.
Doesn't drop things accidentally anymore.
Chooses to pay attention to a person or situation.
Stays focused on something or someone for a while (1 minute).
Becomes aware of their surroundings.
Watches curiously and intently while you do things.
Listens to people talking.
Listens with interest when you speak to them.
Matches sound to object, such as a doorbell with the door.
Follows simple, one-step instructions (like 'Pick up the toy').
Finds their way in familiar places, such as their parent's room.
Completes tasks with two steps, like 'Find your toy, bring it here.'
Pays attention to an adult reading a book for a few minutes.
Recognizes the names of familiar people.
Pairs items with their pictures in books.
Points to or names characters from familiar stories.
Asks for two or three things by their name, like 'bottle' or 'food'.
Puts two words together to make a brief phrase, like 'more cookie'.
Communicates a full idea with one word, like 'park' for 'take me to the park'.
Speaks briefly about recent activities using one or two words.
Names places in pictures, like park, home, market.
Answers simple questions about an image (e.g., if asked 'what color are the leaves?' they respond 'green').
Walks on narrow spaces.
Climbs stairs with an adult, switching feet.
Descends stairs with an adult, switching feet.
Walks up ramps.
Walks backward.
Can climb stairs by holding onto something and using one foot after the other.
Walks down the stairs unassisted, switching feet and using support.
Walks up stairs without help or holding on.
Takes steps using heel-to-toe motion.
Walks down the stairs alone without holding on.
Kicks a ball while being helped to walk.
Kicks a ball while standing.
Runs to a ball and kicks it.
Interacts with moving objects, (for example, kicks a ball that is moving).
Kicks a ball towards a specific direction.
Uses their whole hand to hold a crayon.
Scribbles by moving their entire arm from the shoulder.
Only moves their wrist while scribbling.
Draws lines on paper using their finger.
Draws or paints horizontal lines.
Draws or paints vertical lines.
Can draw or paint in circular motions.
Helps with the dressing and undressing processes by moving the right body parts.
Uses personal care tools like a hairbrush and toothbrush correctly.
Knows how to take off their shoes.
Helps in removing clothes, such as pulling down pants.
Feeds independently with a fork, using the whole hand.
Drinks from a cup with one hand.
Can pull pants down.
Can open a big zipper.
Puts on shoes without laces.
Puts their pants on.
Pours water from a pitcher into a cup with both hands.
Can undo a big button on their clothes.
Puts on a shirt without buttons.
Cuts food with a kid's knife with supervision.
Reacts when they see themselves in a mirror.
When they hear their name, they move toward the person by crawling, walking, or turning in their direction.
Recognizes their reflection in the mirror.
Identifies a boy and a girl in an image.
Spontaneously shows affection towards their friends.
Shows empathy when they see a crying friend (e.g., will try to comfort them).
Shares their toys with other kids.
Plays alongside another child but doesn't interact directly.
Likes playing with friends more than alone.
Solves problems with other kids, like sharing toys or taking turns.
Cooperates with other kids, like working together to achieve something.
Understands the difference between 'big' and 'small'.
Knows the difference between one, two, and many.
Knows the difference between 'front' and 'back'.
Understands what loud and soft volume is. Knows how to apply each, like when to talk quietly.
Differentiates between 'on,' 'over,' and 'under', like putting something under the table when asked.
Knows what certain body parts do, like ears are for hearing.
Identifies three or more numbers with personal importance, like their age or house number.
Understands the difference between 'heavy' and 'light'.
Names or points to tools used in different jobs (like a doctor's stethoscope).
Identifies community helpers (like a doctor, policeman, or firefighter).
Understands when something is long or short.
Recognizes things that are the same and when they're a bit different, like an item that is out of place.
Can open and close all types of lids, like jars, toothpaste, and water bottles.
Stacks 6 or more blocks to make towers.
Rolls small paper or playdough balls with their hands.
Stacks 9 or more blocks.
Rolls playdough to make long strips by using hands or the table.
Grasps and releases objects with precision to build structures with indoor (blocks) and outdoor materials (sticks, leaves).
Names a character's feelings in a story using pictures, like pointing to the happy character.
Can do tasks with three clear steps, like 'Put the apple on the plate, have some water, and then clean your face'.
Completes sentences from familiar books or songs by filling in the blanks.
Recalls bits of a story from the day before.
Calls a friend by their name.
Can say who their friends are among kids they know.
Jumps forward.
Jumps in place with both feet.
Jumps down a small step.
Jumps ahead with both feet at once.
Jumps down from a height of about 18 inches.
Jumps backward.
Hops on one foot for 2 seconds.
Combines nouns and verbs, like 'mommy go'.
Uses words like 'I,' 'me,' and 'you'.
Says plural words (like cars, dogs, and cats).
Says words that rhyme, like cat-hat.
Understands the meaning of 'two' with a finger sign.
Can count when asked to.
Counts from 1 to 30.
Holds up 5 fingers to mean 5.
Moves to the rhythm of music.
Claps or taps an instrument to the rhythm of a song.
Tries to sing along with songs they know.
Looks for an item they dropped on the floor.
Looks for a toy that was just hidden.
Discovers things hidden under blankets or covers.
Searches for hidden toys.
Identifies animals by their sound.
Understands that objects have different shapes, textures, and sizes.
Understands simple rules, like using paint on paper, not the table.
Knows the difference 'up' and 'down.'
Knows the difference between 'inside' and 'outside.'
Finds an object hidden under several covers.
Becomes calm when hearing voices they know.
Responds positively to loving gestures.
Recognizes caregivers.
Smiles when people make eye contact.
Acts differently when around familiar and unfamiliar adults.
Lifts their arms to be carried.
Shows preference for certain people.
Interacts with people they are familiar with by smiling and/or talking.
Feels shy or anxious when meeting new adults.
Expresses love to those familiar, like hugging them.
Knows which things belong to family members, like Mom's purse or Dad's wallet.
